title: Ask Your Leader to Define the Criteria of Success Before Beginning Any Role, Assignment, or Initiative
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note distinguishes between clarifying the tasks and timeline of an assignment and clarifying what the leader will actually consider success at the end. The argument is that even thorough up-front planning conversations often skip this second, backward-looking exercise: asking the leader to describe the triumphant endpoint in detail, including what should not happen along the way. The piece positions this as a simple, low-cost habit -- requesting a criteria-of-success conversation before work begins -- that prevents the common and frustrating experience of completing a project only to learn the leader wanted something different.
points: Task clarity and success-criteria clarity are presented as two distinct, often-conflated conversations.
Asking leaders to describe the end state, working backward, surfaces expectations that forward planning misses.
Leaders describing success often also reveal what resources, people, or timing should be avoided.
No one can read a leader's mind, so requesting this conversation explicitly is framed as essential practice.
The piece recommends never starting a new role or project without first securing this clarity.
quotes: Nothing is more infuriating to team members than reaching the end of an assignment they believe has been successfully completed only to learn the leader is disappointed with the outcome.
Asking a leader to work backward from a successful endpoint, including a careful description of the triumphant finish, creates a very different kind of clarity.
No one can read the mind of a leader to know what they really expect from a role, project, or initiative.
This simple but powerful clarity will often prevent disappointment for both parties at the end of a project or when measuring the effectiveness of a new role.
Avoiding unnecessary distress at the end of an assignment can depend on achieving this clarity. Don’t start a project or accept a new role without it.
